title: CEO Interview with Ajit Prabhu of Quest Global - Semiwiki
gist: Quest Global CEO Ajit Prabhu argues the industry-wide rush to custom ASICs is colliding with a shared-ecosystem constraint: modern fabs are built for high-volume production, not the low-volume custom programs hyperscalers and automakers now want, so the binding scarcity is fab/packaging capacity and domain-specific design talent rather than headcount. His prescription is selectivity about what deserves custom silicon plus outsourcing full-chip ownership at leading-edge nodes to partners.

themes.theme: Custom silicon as a collective constraint

insights.claim: Demand for custom silicon has broadened from chip companies to hyperscalers and automakers, who now see custom ASICs as the clearest path to differentiation because they deliver performance and efficiency standard parts cannot match.
insights.so_what: Broadening ASIC demand supports design-services, IP and advanced-packaging suppliers even where merchant chip volumes are flat.
insights.quote: AI has widened demand across every sector, and companies from hyper-scalers to automakers now see custom silicon as the clearest path to real differentiation.
insights.locator: What is fundamentally changing in the semiconductor industry
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni

insights.claim: Individually rational decisions to pursue custom silicon aggregate into a systemic squeeze on shared ecosystem resources — fab capacity, advanced packaging and specialized talent — so the constraint is collective rather than firm-specific.
insights.so_what: A framework for spotting bottleneck assets: the scarce inputs (packaging, leading-edge capacity, design talent) capture the value, not the ASIC programs themselves.
insights.quote: The pursuit of individual advantage can quietly become a collective constraint.
insights.locator: The challenge is what happens when everyone
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni

insights.claim: Companies that recognize the shared-ecosystem squeeze early and engage suppliers thoughtfully will convert that foresight into competitive advantage over rivals who assume capacity will be there.
insights.so_what: Watch which chip buyers have pre-committed capacity and packaging agreements — that is now a differentiator, not procurement trivia.
insights.locator: The companies that recognize this early
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni

themes.theme: The fab dilemma: economics vs. low-volume ASICs

insights.claim: Modern leading-edge fabs are economically structured for high-volume production and are a poor fit for the low-volume custom programs many companies now need, because retooling for custom ASICs carries real cost and resource demands that are hard to justify at small scale.
insights.so_what: A structural gap that favors foundries/OSATs offering flexible low-volume shuttles and specialty flows — and squeezes long-tail ASIC startups.
insights.quote: Modern fabs are built for high-volume production, not the low-volume custom programs that many companies now need.
insights.locator: There’s a growing strain across the semiconductor value chain
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni

insights.claim: The gap between fab economics and market demand for custom silicon is an underdiscussed structural problem that cannot be solved by buying more capacity.
insights.so_what: Capex headlines are not the fix; the tradable insight is in who arbitrages low-volume demand against high-volume fab economics.
insights.quote: You can’t out-build this demand, so you have to out-think it.
insights.locator: So, the smarter question isn’t how to buy more capacity
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni

insights.claim: AI-assisted design tools help with the custom-silicon bottleneck but solve only pieces of a much larger puzzle that includes fab capacity, packaging and expertise.
insights.so_what: Tempering signal for EDA-AI narratives: tooling productivity does not relieve the physical capacity constraint.
insights.quote: AI-assisted design tools help, but they solve pieces of a much larger puzzle.
insights.locator: So, the smarter question isn’t how to buy more capacity
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni

themes.theme: Talent as domain depth, not headcount

insights.claim: The semiconductor talent shortage is misdiagnosed as a numbers problem when the binding constraint is domain expertise: designing a custom ASIC for a hyperscale data center is a fundamentally different discipline from designing one for automotive or medical use.
insights.so_what: Engineering-services firms with vertical depth command pricing power that generic staffing bodies cannot; headcount metrics mislead.
insights.quote: Designing a custom ASIC for a hyperscale data center is fundamentally different from designing one for automotive or medical use. These aren’t variations of a single skill. They’re distinct disciplines built over the years.
insights.locator: As custom silicon becomes harder to pursue in isolation
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni

insights.claim: Organizations navigating the custom-silicon wave successfully are outsourcing entire design programs end to end so their internal teams can concentrate on critical IP and long-term innovation rather than execution.
insights.so_what: Structural tailwind for full-chip-ownership design-services providers as chip buyers narrow internal scope to differentiating IP.
insights.quote: By partnering with those who can manage entire programs end to end, they free their own teams to focus on critical IP and long-term innovation.
insights.locator: No single company can master all of it alone
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni

insights.claim: Quest Global has grown from a two-person startup founded in 1997 to over 23,000 engineers across 20 countries, serving Aerospace & Defense, Automotive, Energy, Hi-Tech, MedTech & Healthcare, Rail and Semiconductors.
insights.so_what: Sizes an independent pure-play engineering-services competitor in the outsourced chip-design market.
insights.locator: A mission-driven entrepreneur, Ajit believes culture
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni

insights.claim: Quest Global claims it supports semiconductor clients from advanced design services all the way to full-chip ownership at leading-edge nodes, positioning itself above pure capacity augmentation.
insights.so_what: Full-chip ownership is a higher-margin, stickier tier of engineering services than staff augmentation — watch mix shift.
insights.quote: We support everything from advanced design services to full-chip ownership at leading-edge nodes
insights.locator: That is especially relevant in semiconductors
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni

insights.claim: Prabhu dismisses scale, capacity and talent pools as table stakes rather than differentiation in engineering services, arguing the industry's standard pitch is commoditized.
insights.so_what: Implies price/margin compression for undifferentiated engineering-services vendors competing on headcount.
insights.quote: Those things matter. But they are table stakes, not a strategy.
insights.locator: What does the competitive landscape look like
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni

insights.claim: Quest Global deliberately builds fewer, longer-term client relationships rather than chasing volume, treating relationship depth as a prerequisite for owning a design problem.
insights.so_what: A concentrated-customer model: higher revenue durability but also higher client-concentration risk.
insights.quote: It’s why we choose to build fewer, longer-term relationships rather than chase volume.
insights.locator: That kind of partnership requires real depth
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni

insights.claim: Prabhu frames AI in engineering as a multiplier of engineers rather than a replacement, and explicitly ties that choice to business strategy: replacement tools shrink the firm while multiplier tools expand it.
insights.so_what: Signals engineering-services firms will not price AI as headcount deflation — watch whether clients accept that or demand rate cuts.
insights.quote: A tool that replaces people makes you smaller. A tool that multiplies them makes you bolder.
insights.locator: How are you keeping pace with technology advancements
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni

insights.claim: AI-driven design methodologies and advanced-node engineering are already compressing design cycles and shrinking the margin for error, so competitive advantage shifts to firms that pair the best engineers with the best tools rather than the ones with the most engineers.
insights.so_what: Revenue-per-engineer, not engineer count, becomes the metric to track in design-services names.
insights.quote: In that world, the winners won’t be the ones with the most engineers.
insights.locator: We are also strengthening our capabilities through targeted acquisitions
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni

insights.claim: Quest Global is using targeted acquisitions to add capability aligned to where customers are heading, alongside organic investment in AI-enabled engineering and global talent.
insights.so_what: An active acquirer in engineering services — relevant for private targets in digital engineering and chip design.
insights.quote: We are also strengthening our capabilities through targeted acquisitions
insights.locator: We are also strengthening our capabilities
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni

insights.claim: The largest growth opportunity Prabhu identifies is the convergence of AI, digital engineering and intelligent products, driving demand for partners who can co-create innovation rather than execute discrete tasks.
insights.so_what: Outcome-based engineering contracts should grow faster than time-and-materials — a mix indicator for the sector.
insights.locator: What do you think will be the biggest growth opportunities
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
